question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
After Analia's Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls both Corrupted Conscience and Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," so Analia gains control of Nico's Corrupted Conscience (an Aura is a permanent, so it's a legal target for Lay Claim's enchant ability) [303.4e]. Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature" — the "you" in an Aura's text means that Aura's controller at the time the effect is applied, which is now Analia [Lay Claim ruling #0]. So Corrupted Conscience's control-change effect now hands Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia instead of Nico.

Control-changing effects are applied in layer 2 of the layer system, and they're recalculated continuously from the actual objects, so as soon as Analia becomes Corrupted Conscience's controller, Bane Alley Blackguard's controller updates too [613.1b]. Note that Analia is also Bane Alley Blackguard's owner and its default controller, so nothing odd happens even if Corrupted Conscience later leaves the battlefield [110.2].

Also note the general principle in the other direction: gaining control of a creature does not give you control of Auras attached to it, and vice versa [303.4e][Lay Claim ruling #0] — here the control change flows only because Corrupted Conscience's own text grants control to its controller.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if a player leaves the game, control effects they provided end and objects can be exiled or leave the game [800.4a][800.4c]. No timing ambiguity affects the outcome here — I've assumed Lay Claim resolved successfully and both Auras remain on the battlefield.

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Iroas, God of Victory is a creature after Starfield of Nyx resolves, and it's a 4/4.

Why:

1. Devotion. Devotion to red and white counts mana symbols that are red, white, or both among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls (700.5a). Iroas, God of Victory's own {2}{R}{W} contributes 2, and Alan's devotion to white is 2 — nowhere near seven. Starfield of Nyx costs {4}{W}, adding one white symbol, so devotion to red and white is still well under seven. So Iroas, God of Victory's own ability "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature" is active. Note devotion is calculated after copy/control/text-changing effects but before other characteristic-modifying effects (700.5a), so Starfield of Nyx's type-changing doesn't alter the count.

2. Layer 4 (types). Two effects apply: Iroas, God of Victory's ability removing the creature type, and Starfield of Nyx's "each other non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature in addition to its other types" (Alan controls five enchantments: Iroas, God of Victory, three others, and Starfield of Nyx itself). Neither depends on the other under the 613.8a test, so they apply in timestamp order (613.1, 613.6). Starfield of Nyx's effect has the later timestamp, so it applies last and Iroas, God of Victory ends up a Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.

3. Layer 7b (base P/T). Starfield of Nyx sets base power and base toughness each equal to mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana value is 4, so it's 4/4, not its printed 7/4 (613.1g, 613.4a, 302.4c). This setting effect applies in layer 7b regardless of what happened in layer 4 (613.6), and would apply even if the permanent weren't a creature at the time (208.3a).

Timing assumption: I'm treating the question as asking about the state immediately after Starfield of Nyx resolves, with Starfield of Nyx's timestamp later than Iroas, God of Victory's. That's necessarily the case here since Iroas, God of Victory was already on the battlefield. If Alan later stops controlling five enchantments, Starfield of Nyx's effect switches off and Iroas, God of Victory reverts to a non-creature 7/4 enchantment; if devotion to red and white ever reaches seven, it would be a creature either way (7/4 base, still overwritten to 4/4 by Starfield of Nyx while that's active).

Player count doesn't matter here — devotion counts only permanents Alan controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Alex activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nadia with it. Nadia doesn't block it and then casts [Summoning Trap], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Nadia loses 1 life. Because Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield before the combat damage step, Alex's Inkmoth Nexus (an opponent's creature from Nadia's perspective) loses infect, so its 1 combat damage is dealt as ordinary damage and simply causes Nadia to lose 1 life — no poison counters.

Details and assumed timing: I'm assuming Summoning Trap was cast and resolved during the declare blockers step (after Nadia declined to block), so Melira, Sylvok Outcast is already on the battlefield when the combat damage step begins. In that step, Alex announces that the unblocked Inkmoth Nexus assigns its 1 combat damage to Nadia (510.1, 703.4k), then that damage is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack (510.2, 703.4m). Since Melira, Sylvok Outcast's static ability strips infect from creatures Nadia's opponents control, the damage is processed into normal results — 1 life lost, not a poison counter (120.3, 120.4b–d, 702.90b).

Even if you instead read the timing so that Melira, Sylvok Outcast somehow wasn't present until after damage, the result for Nadia is still no poison: Melira, Sylvok Outcast's first ability says "You can't get poison counters," so poison counters could never be given to Nadia while it's out (Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1). And if Melira, Sylvok Outcast were not on the battlefield at all when damage was dealt, Nadia would instead get 1 poison counter and lose no life.

Note also that Inkmoth Nexus is still a land as well as a creature, and abilities that merely check whether damage was dealt would still see the damage (Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1).

Multiplayer: nothing changes. Combat damage assignment happens in APNAP order (703.4k) and Nadia is the defending player being attacked; other opponents are unaffected. Under the shared team turns option the active team announces attacker damage assignment first (805.10f), but the outcome here is the same.

question: Nathaniel controls a [Melira, Sylvok Outcast]. Ari activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nathaniel with it. Nathaniel doesn't block. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus deals 1 combat damage to Nathaniel, and that damage has no result at all: Nathaniel loses no life and gets no poison counters.

Why: Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "Creatures your opponents control lose infect," but Inkmoth Nexus's own activated ability grants infect with a later timestamp, and as Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1 explains, these two effects are applied in timestamp order with the most recent winning — so the animated Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 with flying and infect. (Ruling #3 covers the different case of an already-infect creature entering later, which does lose infect.)

Then in the combat damage step, unblocked Inkmoth Nexus assigns its damage to the player it's attacking [510.1b], and that damage is dealt [510.2, 703.4m]. Processing it into results [120.4c]: because the source has infect, the damage does not cause Nathaniel to lose life; instead it would give him poison counters [702.90b, 120.3b]. But Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "You can't get poison counters," so no poison counter is given either. Net effect: zero.

Important caveat: the damage was still dealt. Abilities that check whether damage was dealt (lifelink, "whenever this creature deals damage to a player" triggers) still see it, per Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1.

This all happens the same way with two players or at a multiplayer table; Melira, Sylvok Outcast protects only Nathaniel and creatures he controls, so other players' creatures dealt damage by Inkmoth Nexus would get -1/-1 counters normally.

question: Autumn controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue" and [Sword of Body and Mind]. Nico casts [Gift of Tusks] targeting the Painter's Servant. After it resolves, what happens if Autumn tries to equip Painter's Servant with Sword of Body and Mind?
answer:
The equip works: Sword of Body and Mind attaches to Painter's Servant and stays attached.

Why: Equip {2} means "Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Painter's Servant is still a creature (Gift of Tusks makes it a green Elephant with base power and toughness 3/3), it's controlled by Autumn, and an Equipment can legally be attached to a creature [301.5c], so the ability has a legal target and resolves.

The key point is what Gift of Tusks did. Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities, so its color-changing ability ("All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors") is gone [113.10]. Sword of Body and Mind is therefore just a colorless artifact again, not blue. Sword of Body and Mind grants the equipped creature protection from green and from blue, and protection would force an Equipment with the named quality to become unattached as a state-based action [702.16d, 704.1] — but Sword of Body and Mind is neither green nor blue, so nothing unattaches. (Protection also doesn't care that Painter's Servant itself is green; the quality is checked against the Equipment.) Painter's Servant ends up a 5/5 green Elephant with protection from green and from blue.

Contrast: if Painter's Servant still had its ability naming blue, Sword of Body and Mind would be blue, and the moment it became attached the protection-from-blue it grants would immediately unattach it as a state-based action, leaving it on the battlefield unattached [702.16d, 704.1, 301.5c]. Note also that if some other effect gives Painter's Servant an ability after Gift of Tusks has resolved, it keeps that ability [Gift of Tusks ruling #0], but the original color-changing ability is not coming back this turn.

Timing assumption: Gift of Tusks has already fully resolved before the equip ability is activated, as stated. If instead Gift of Tusks were cast and resolved after Sword of Body and Mind was already attached, the result is the same end state — Sword of Body and Mind stops being blue and remains attached. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up 5/4.

Why: characteristics are worked out in the CR 613 layer system (613.1, 613.1g), and abilities are settled in layer 6 before power/toughness in layer 7.

Layer 6 (abilities), in timestamp order (613.7):
- Crowd's Favor granted Grizzly Bears first strike.
- Archetype of Courage, cast later by Amia, says creatures your opponents control "lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." With the later timestamp, it strips that granted ability. Per 113.12, a granted ability like this can be removed by another effect. So after Archetype of Courage resolves, Grizzly Bears has no abilities at all.

Layer 7c (modify power/toughness, 613.4c, 302.4c):
- Muraganda Petroglyphs ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") now applies again, because Grizzly Bears has no abilities: 2/2 → 4/4.
- Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 still applies — that part of the effect is independent of the first strike grant and is not removed: 4/4 → 5/4.

So the Petroglyphs bonus "turns back on" the instant first strike is stripped; 613.5 confirms these recalculations are continuous and instantaneous.

Timing note: this assumes Crowd's Favor fully resolved before Archetype of Courage was cast, as stated. If instead Archetype of Courage were already on the battlefield when Crowd's Favor resolved, Grizzly Bears still couldn't gain first strike ("can't have or gain"), so it would still be 5/4.

Player count doesn't matter here: Archetype of Courage affects creatures each of its controller's opponents controls, so in a multiplayer game it strips first strike from Grizzly Bears and from every other opponent's creatures identically.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
No — Murmuring Bosk is not a creature. It's a nonbasic Land with the single land subtype Mountain, with only the ability "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain (its printed abilities are also gone under Blood Moon's effect, which sets nonbasic lands to be Mountains).

Why: both Blood Moon and Life and Limb are type-changing continuous effects that apply in CR 613's layer 4, so they'd normally be ordered by timestamp — but a dependency overrides timestamp order (CR 613.8a). Applying Blood Moon changes what Life and Limb applies to (it strips the Forest subtype from Murmuring Bosk), so Life and Limb depends on Blood Moon and Blood Moon applies first even though Life and Limb has the earlier timestamp. After Blood Moon, Murmuring Bosk's only land type is Mountain, not Forest, so Life and Limb — which affects only Forests and Saprolings — never applies to it. Consequently it also doesn't get Life and Limb's green color (layer 5) or its 1/1 power/toughness (layer 7b), and it doesn't gain the Saproling creature type.

Background: Murmuring Bosk is a nonbasic land even though it has the Forest land type, because it lacks the "basic" supertype (CR 305.8, 205.4c, and Murmuring Bosk ruling #0) — that's exactly why Blood Moon catches it. If Murmuring Bosk were instead a basic Forest, Blood Moon wouldn't touch it and Life and Limb would make it a 1/1 green Saproling creature land (Life and Limb ruling #3; each subtype stays correlated to its proper card type, CR 205.3c).

The order the permanents entered doesn't change this result here, since the dependency, not the timestamp, decides the order. This analysis is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table — nothing about it depends on the number of opponents.

question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
No. Angelica's Sheltered Thicket is not a creature ">Blood Moon" wins here " it is just a nonbasic land with the single land subtype Mountain.

Why: Both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are type-changing continuous effects, so both are applied in layer 4 of the layer system (CR 613.6 describes how the parts of such effects are sorted into layers). Blood Moon sets the land subtypes of every nonbasic land to just Mountain, which strips Sheltered Thicket's printed Forest subtype. Life and Limb only applies to Forests and Saprolings, so once Blood Moon has applied, Sheltered Thicket is neither, and Life and Limb never starts applying to it at all " not in layer 4 (no Creature type, no Saproling subtype), not in layer 5 (not green), and not in layer 7b (no 1/1 power/toughness).

This is also a genuine dependency, not just a timestamp result: Blood Moon's effect changes what Life and Limb applies to, which is exactly the CR 613.8a dependency test, so Blood Moon is applied first regardless. Here it doesn't matter, since Blood Moon also entered first.

A couple of consequences worth acting on: Sheltered Thicket has no power or toughness, because a noncreature permanent has none (CR 208.3a); it can't attack or block (CR 506.3f); and it isn't affected by summoning sickness because it isn't a creature. Note also that CR 205.3c/205.4b confirm subtypes stay correlated to their card type " Forest is a land type, Saproling is a creature type " which is why losing the Forest land type is what shuts Life and Limb off. If Blood Moon ever leaves the battlefield, Sheltered Thicket's Forest subtype returns and Life and Limb immediately makes it a 1/1 green Saproling creature Forest land (per Life and Limb ruling #3).

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Short answer: Alfred's Saproling token ends up a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a land — and because of Blood Moon that land is a Mountain rather than a Forest, so it has "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}."

Why:

1. The token as created is only a 1/1 green Saproling creature token; a token has no characteristics beyond what its creating effect defined [111.3], and nothing gave it the "basic" supertype, so it is not a basic land — any land that lacks the basic supertype is a nonbasic land [Nonbasic Land], [Basic].

2. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." So the Saproling token gains the card type land and the land subtype Forest while keeping the creature type Saproling; each subtype stays correlated with its proper type — Saproling is not a land type and Forest is not a creature type [Life and Limb ruling #3]. It is also a creature that entered as a land creature [Life and Limb ruling #1], and it's subject to summoning sickness per Life and Limb's own text.

3. Now that Life and Limb has made the token a land, and it is a nonbasic land, Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies and sets its land subtype to Mountain, replacing Forest. Its creature type Saproling and its supertypes are untouched by that land-type change [205.4b].

4. As a Mountain it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Mountain], [305.6]; it does not have Forest's "{T}: Add {G}" [Forest], because it no longer has the Forest subtype.

So: a 1/1 green Saproling creature Mountain land that taps for {R}, summoning-sick the turn it arrived.

Assumption and a caveat on ordering: Blood Moon entered before Life and Limb. Type-changing effects from both are applied in the same layer, and the parts of each effect apply in their appropriate layers [613.6]. The reason Blood Moon still "catches" the token even though it has the earlier timestamp is that Blood Moon can only tell what it applies to after Life and Limb has made the token a land — the exact numbered rules on timestamps and dependency were not included in the context provided to me, so I'm grounding that step on the plain reading of the two cards' text. If you instead applied the two effects strictly by timestamp with no dependency, the token would keep the Forest subtype and tap for {G}.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count, so it's the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

answer:
Alex's Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain, and its only mana ability is "{T}: Add {R}" — it does not tap for {G}.

- Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." So the Saproling token gains the land card type and the land subtype Forest, while keeping creature/Saproling. Card types and subtypes stay correlated: Forest is a land type, Saproling is a creature type [Life and Limb ruling #3].
- Being a Forest land, the token would normally have the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6] [Forest].
- The token has no "basic" supertype (tokens only have characteristics defined by the effect that created them [111.3], and Life and Limb grants types, not supertypes [205.4b]), so it is a nonbasic land [Nonbasic Land] [Basic].

Blood Moon changes land types only, so the creature type Saproling and the 1/1 green creature status from Life and Limb remain.

One consequence worth noting: since it entered as a land creature, abilities that trigger when a land enters the battlefield triggered [Life and Limb ruling #1], and it's subject to summoning sickness, so it can't attack or use {T} abilities (including tapping for {R}) until it has been under Alex's control since their most recent turn began (per Life and Limb's own text).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Both end up as 1/1 green Saproling Mountain land creatures whose only ability is "{T}: Add {R}."

How it gets there (timestamp order: Life and Limb, then Blood Moon; both are type-changing effects in layer 4, and since each changes what the other applies to, they're mutually dependent and simply applied in timestamp order):

Sapseep Forest (Land — Forest, nonbasic, no "basic" supertype per 205.4c):
- Layer 4, Life and Limb (earlier): as a Forest, it becomes a Saproling creature in addition to its other types — Land Creature — Forest Saproling. Subtypes stay correlated to their card types: Forest is the land type, Saproling the creature type [205.3c, Life and Limb ruling #3].
- Layer 4, Blood Moon (later): Sapseep Forest is still a nonbasic land, so it becomes a Mountain, losing the Forest land type. It keeps its creature type Saproling and its creature card type (Blood Moon only sets land subtypes) [Blood Moon ruling #2, 205.3i].
- Layer 5, Life and Limb: green.
- Layer 6, Blood Moon: it loses all its other abilities — the intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" from Forest, "This land enters tapped," and "{G}, {T}: You gain 1 life" — and has "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain [Blood Moon ruling #2, 305.6, 107.4a].
- Layer 7b, Life and Limb: 1/1.
Result: a green 1/1 Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}." (Note the "enters tapped" clause already happened when it entered, before Blood Moon stripped it, assuming Blood Moon was on the battlefield only from the timing you gave; if Blood Moon had been out first, Sapseep Forest would have entered untapped [614.12, 614.1c].)

The Saproling token (base 1/1 green Creature — Saproling, no abilities [111.3]):
- Layer 4, Life and Limb: it's a Saproling, so it becomes a Forest land in addition to its other types — Land Creature — Forest Saproling. It's a nonbasic land, because tokens don't have the "basic" supertype [205.4c, Life and Limb ruling #1].
- Layer 4, Blood Moon: now a nonbasic land, so it becomes a Mountain and loses the Forest land type; it stays a Saproling creature.
- Layer 6: it loses the "{T}: Add {G}" it briefly had and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2, 305.6].
- Layers 5/7b, Life and Limb: green, 1/1.
Result: identical — a green 1/1 Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}."

Practical notes: both are creatures Aubriella hasn't controlled since her turn began (summoning sickness), so she can't pay the {T} in their mana abilities yet [Life and Limb ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Cinder Glade is just a Land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}", nothing else. The Saproling token is a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}" (no {G} ability).

Why:

Both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") apply in layer 4 (type-changing), so normally timestamp order (Blood Moon first) governs — but dependency (CR 613.6/613.5-style layer application, and the dependency test) matters here, and it happens to point the same way for Cinder Glade and the other way for the token.

Cinder Glade (nonbasic land, printed Land — Mountain Forest):
- Blood Moon applies first: it's a nonbasic land, so it becomes a Mountain and loses its other land types (Forest) and its abilities, per [Blood Moon ruling #2]. Having the Mountain subtype gives it the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6].
- Life and Limb then checks for Forests/Saprolings. Cinder Glade is neither anymore, so Life and Limb never applies to it. Its "enters tapped unless..." text and its {G} ability are gone.
- Result: an untapped-relevant, non-creature Land — Mountain, colorless, with only "{T}: Add {R}".

The 1/1 green Saproling token (a token has only the characteristics its creating effect defined [111.3]):
- Life and Limb applies to it because it's a Saproling: in layer 4 it becomes a Saproling creature and a Forest land in addition to its other types [Life and Limb ruling #3]; layer 5 keeps it green; layer 7b sets it 1/1.
- Now it is a land with no "basic" supertype, i.e. a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon applies to it in layer 4 even though Blood Moon has the earlier timestamp: Life and Limb's effect changes what Blood Moon applies to, so Blood Moon depends on it and is applied afterward. Blood Moon changes its land types to Mountain only, stripping Forest and the "{T}: Add {G}" that came with it, and it gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, Blood Moon ruling #2].
- Blood Moon only alters land subtypes, so the creature card type and the creature subtype Saproling survive (subtypes stay correlated to their card types [205.3c]), and the layer 5 color and layer 7b power/toughness from Life and Limb still apply [613.6].
- Result: a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling that taps for {R}. It's subject to summoning sickness, so it can't use that tap ability the turn it entered unless it has haste.

Assumption on ordering: I'm reading "entered in that order" as Blood Moon's timestamp being earliest and Life and Limb's next. Swapping the two enchantments' timestamps wouldn't change either result, because the dependency relationships above force the same application order.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's identical at a two-player or multiplayer table, since both enchantments affect the permanents regardless of controller.

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling Forest artifact land creature (still an Artifact with its own abilities), and it's subject to summoning sickness.

How the effects stack up, in timestamp order (March of the Machines, then Xenograft, then Life and Limb — which also happens to be the dependency order, since Xenograft only applies once Ore-Rich Stalactite is a creature, and Life and Limb only applies once it's a Saproling):

- Layer 4 (types): March of the Machines makes Ore-Rich Stalactite, a noncreature artifact, an artifact creature. Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes it a Saproling in addition to its other types. Because Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling, Life and Limb applies to it, making it a Saproling creature and a Forest land in addition to its other types. It is now an artifact land creature — a combination subject to the rules for both artifacts and lands [Artifact Land].
- Layer 5 (color): Life and Limb makes it green (in addition to nothing else — it becomes green rather than colorless).
- Layer 7b (setting power/toughness): March of the Machines sets its power and toughness to its mana value (2/2), then Life and Limb, with the later timestamp, sets them to 1/1. Final result: 1/1 [613.6].

Because it has the land card type and the basic land type Forest, Ore-Rich Stalactite gains the intrinsic mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6], in addition to its printed "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" and its craft ability. It is still not a basic land (it lacks the basic supertype), so it's a nonbasic land with the Forest subtype [Nonbasic Land]. Being a creature, it can't be tapped for mana or crafted-away using {T} while it has summoning sickness unless it has been under Alannah's control since her most recent turn began — Life and Limb itself reminds you it's affected by summoning sickness.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Both lands are unaffected by Magus of the Moon: Furycalm Snarl is still just a Land (no subtypes) with "As this land enters, you may reveal a Mountain or Plains card from your hand. If you don't, this land enters tapped" and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}", and Crosis's Catacombs is still a Land — Lair with its enters-trigger and "{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}".

Why: Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Magus of the Moon is a creature, so Humility applies to it. In the layer system (CR 613.1), ability-adding/removing effects are applied in layer 6 in timestamp order; Humility entered before Magus of the Moon, so Humility's removal is applied to Magus of the Moon and Magus of the Moon loses "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" (it also becomes a 1/1 Human Wizard in layer 7). Because that ability is gone before it ever begins applying, it generates no type-changing effect in layer 4 at all. CR 613.6 (an effect keeps applying even if its source ability is later removed) doesn't rescue it — Humility's timestamp is earlier, so the Magus of the Moon effect never started applying.

So, concretely:
- Furycalm Snarl: colorless (lands have no color), card type Land, no supertypes, no land subtypes (per Furycalm Snarl ruling #1 the "Snarl" itself has no land subtypes), both of its printed abilities intact, no power/toughness.
- Crosis's Catacombs: colorless, card type Land, subtype Lair, both printed abilities intact, no power/toughness. Its enters-trigger already resolved when it entered (you either returned a non-Lair land or sacrificed it); the question implies it's still on the battlefield.
- (Magus of the Moon itself: a 1/1 red Human Wizard creature with no abilities.)

Timing assumption: the stated order — Furycalm Snarl, then Humility, then Magus of the Moon, then Crosis's Catacombs — is the timestamp order. If Magus of the Moon had somehow gotten the later timestamp (e.g., Humility entered after Magus of the Moon and then Magus of the Moon re-entered), Magus of the Moon's ability would apply and both lands would be Mountains with only "{T}: Add {R}". This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games since only Ainsley's permanents are involved.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
No \u2014 Volrath's Shapeshifter does not have flying. It is a 6/6 blue Illusion creature named Mistform Skyreaver with only the ability "{2}: Discard a card."

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that as long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the "full text" of that card plus "{2}: Discard a card." Per [612.6], "full text" copies the other object's name, mana cost, color, power, toughness, type line and text box \ifty\u2014 i.e., whatever text that graveyard card actually has. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so while Mistform Skyreaver sits in Aiden's graveyard it has no abilities at all \u2014 no flying and no "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice." The full text Volrath's Shapeshifter picks up therefore contains no abilities to grant.

What Volrath's Shapeshifter does still get: the name Mistform Skyreaver, mana cost {5}{U}{U}, blue, Creature \u2014 Illusion, and 6/6 (Yixlid Jailer only strips abilities, not name, cost, color, types, or power/toughness). It also keeps "{2}: Discard a card." \u2014 that ability is granted by Volrath's Shapeshifter's own text on the battlefield, not copied from the graveyard card, and [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1] confirms it keeps that granted ability in addition to the copied ones. Running the layer bookkeeping (type change in layer 4, ability changes in layer 6, P/T in layer 7b) gives exactly that result.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield at the same time you're checking Volrath's Shapeshifter's characteristics. If Yixlid Jailer leaves the battlefield, Mistform Skyreaver's abilities come back immediately and Volrath's Shapeshifter would then have flying (and the {1} type-changing ability) for as long as that card is the top card of the graveyard \u2014 this is a continuously re-evaluated static effect, not something locked in.

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Nickolas can't tap Dryad Arbor for {G} while Overwhelming Splendor enchants him.

Why: Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad, so it's a creature Nickolas controls, and Overwhelming Splendor says "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Its mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" isn't printed text — it's the intrinsic ability every object with the Forest land subtype has (305.6) — but intrinsic abilities are still abilities, and they're granted/applied in layer 6 just like the removal. Running the layer system: layer 6 first adds the Forest intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" (earlier timestamp), then Overwhelming Splendor's later-timestamped effect removes all abilities, leaving Dryad Arbor with no abilities; layer 7b then sets its base power/toughness to 1/1. Result: a green 1/1 Land Creature — Forest Dryad with no abilities and no way to produce mana.

Two notes:
- Overwhelming Splendor's second sentence ("Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities") would not have stopped this on its own, since "{T}: Add {G}" is a mana ability (605.1, 605.2). The blocker is purely that the ability no longer exists.
- If something grants Dryad Arbor an ability after Overwhelming Splendor became attached — e.g. a later effect giving it a mana ability — it keeps that ability [Overwhelming Splendor ruling #5], and Nickolas could use it. Likewise, if Dryad Arbor were somehow not a creature, it would keep the Forest mana ability.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dryad Arbor was already on the battlefield when Overwhelming Splendor resolved, as stated. That doesn't change anything here — a Dryad Arbor played later would also enter and immediately lose its abilities, since Overwhelming Splendor's effect applies continuously to all creatures Nickolas controls. Only ability-granting effects with a timestamp later than Overwhelming Splendor survive.

Player count doesn't matter: Overwhelming Splendor enchants a single player (Nickolas), so the answer is the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one; other players' creatures and lands are unaffected.

question: Nico controls [Yixlid Jailer]. Achilles uses [Past in Flames] to give [Deadly Complication] in their graveyard Flashback. Is Achilles able to cast Deadly Complication from their graveyard to destroy Yixlid Jailer?
answer:
No. Achilles can't cast Deadly Complication from their graveyard while Nico's Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield.

Why: Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That card text applies to Deadly Complication while it's in Achilles's graveyard, and it overrides the general expectation that a granted ability would work there. Flashback is a keyword ability — specifically, a static ability that functions while the card is in a player's graveyard, meaning "You may cast this card from your graveyard ... by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" [702.34a], [702.1]. Past in Flames grants each instant and sorcery card in Achilles's graveyard exactly that ability. Because Yixlid Jailer strips all abilities from cards in graveyards, Deadly Complication has no flashback ability there, so there is no permission to cast it from the graveyard, and Achilles isn't legally allowed to begin casting it [601.2b]. This matches Yixlid Jailer ruling #0: if a card's own ability (such as flashback) is what allows casting it from the graveyard, Yixlid Jailer stops that ability. That's true whether the flashback was printed on the card or granted by Past in Flames — the ability still lives on the graveyard card.

Contrast: if some other object's effect said "you may cast Deadly Complication from your graveyard," that permission comes from elsewhere, and per the same ruling the casting would work (the first step being moving it to the stack, where alternative/additional costs could apply).

Timing note: I'm assuming Yixlid Jailer is already on the battlefield when Achilles wants to cast Deadly Complication. Past in Flames still resolves and grants flashback until end of turn to the cards in the graveyard at that time [Past in Flames ruling #3]; if Yixlid Jailer later leaves the battlefield during that same turn, Deadly Complication regains the granted flashback and Achilles could then cast it (following normal sorcery timing, [Past in Flames ruling #10]) — but of course it would then have nothing to destroy unless another target exists. Targeting Nico's Yixlid Jailer would also be committing a crime [700.13].

This works the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer; Yixlid Jailer affects cards in all graveyards, so no player's granted flashback functions.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Direct answer: Swab Goblin becomes a 4/4 red-and-white Kithkin Creature named Figure of Destiny with Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities (mana cost {R/W}). Watchwolf becomes a 0/4 red-and-white Treefolk Creature named Figure of Destiny with no abilities (mana cost {R/W}).

Why:

1. Mirrorweave's copy effect applies in layer 1 (CR 613.1a, 613.2a). A copy uses only the copiable values of Figure of Destiny — the values derived from its printed text: name, mana cost {R/W}, card type Creature, subtype Kithkin, rules text (the three activated abilities), and printed power/toughness 1/1 (CR 707.2a). Color comes along because it's derived from the mana cost, so both copies are red and white.

2. The fact that Aspen already activated Figure of Destiny's third ability does NOT get copied. That ability created a type-changing/base-P-T continuous effect in layers 4 and 7b; such non-copiable effects are explicitly excluded from copiable values (CR 707.2a, 613.2c). So the copies are 1/1 Kithkin, not 8/8 Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatars with flying and first strike. (Figure of Destiny itself is unchanged — Mirrorweave says "each other creature.")

3. Swab Goblin: Pack's Favor's +3/+3 is a layer 7c effect, not a copiable value, so it survives the copy and still applies to that same permanent: 1/1 base becomes 4/4. Note Pack's Favor's convoke doesn't change any of this. Result: 4/4 Kithkin named Figure of Destiny, red and white, with the three {R/W} activation abilities (which Aspen may activate anew; "this creature" refers to that object, per CR 201.5b).

4. Watchwolf: Lignify is still attached (the Aura's object didn't change, just its characteristics). Its effects are outside layer 1, so they apply after the copy: layer 4 makes it a Treefolk (overwriting Kithkin), layer 6 removes all abilities (so the three activated abilities are gone), and layer 7b sets base power/toughness 0/4. Lignify overrides even characteristic-defining abilities that would set P/T or creature types (Lignify ruling #5). Result: 0/4 Treefolk named Figure of Destiny, red and white, no abilities. It's a Creature — Treefolk only; it's not a Wolf anymore.

Timing assumption: Pack's Favor fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. If instead Mirrorweave resolved first and Pack's Favor second, the outcome for Swab Goblin would be identical (7c is applied after layer 1 either way).

Player count doesn't matter here — all the objects are Aspen's, and no provided rule changes with more than two players.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a black Goblin Zombie 4/2 — yes, it gets +1/+1 from Dralnu's Crusade.

Why: Conspiracy, with "Goblin" chosen, makes creatures Allison controls the chosen type, and affected creatures lose all their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]. So Leopard-Spotted Jiao loses Beast and is just a Goblin. Both Conspiracy and Dralnu's Crusade change subtypes (the same layer), and although Dralnu's Crusade has the earlier timestamp, its effect depends on Conspiracy's: applying Conspiracy changes what Dralnu's Crusade applies to, so Conspiracy is applied first. Then Dralnu's Crusade sees a Goblin and adds Zombie in addition to its other creature types [302.3, 205.3m].

Dralnu's Crusade's other effects then apply to Leopard-Spotted Jiao because it is now a Goblin: it becomes black only, not black in addition to red [Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0], and it gets +1/+1, making it 4/2 from its printed 3/1.

Note Conspiracy only changes creature types; it doesn't replace uses of creature types in card text [Conspiracy ruling #0], but Dralnu's Crusade's "All Goblins" checks actual creature types, which Leopard-Spotted Jiao now has. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since Conspiracy affects only creatures Allison controls.

question: Alaina has seven cards in their hand and controls [Recycle]. They cast [Trusted Advisor]. After that resolves, what is Alaina's maximum hand size?
answer:
Alaina's maximum hand size is four.

Hand-size modifiers apply in timestamp order. Recycle entered the battlefield first and sets "Your maximum hand size is two." Trusted Advisor entered later and says "Your maximum hand size is increased by two," so it modifies the value already set by Recycle: 2 + 2 = 4 ([Recycle ruling #2], [Trusted Advisor ruling #0]). (Had the order been reversed — Trusted Advisor first, then Recycle — the maximum would simply be two, because Recycle's later effect overwrites the number.)

Having seven cards in hand right now is fine: maximum hand size only matters during the cleanup step of Alaina's own turn, when the active player discards down to their maximum ([402.2], [514.1], [703.4n], [Recycle ruling #1]). So on Alaina's next cleanup step, they would discard down to four cards. At any other time Alaina may hold any number of cards ([402.2]).

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since these effects only affect Alaina.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.10: Some continuous effects affect players rather than objects. For example, an effect might give a player protection from red. All such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects’ characteristics. See also the rules for timestamp order and dependency (rules 613.7 and 613.8).
gold_text.613.7: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp.

cited_text.402.2: Each player has a maximum hand size, which is normally seven cards. A player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step, the player must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size.
cited_text.514.1: First, if the active player’s hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack.
cited_text.703.4n: The turn-based actions are as follows: Immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player’s hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. See rule 514.1.

answer_gold: Four. Recycle sets the maximum hand size to two, and Trusted Advisor then modifies that maximum hand size by adding two to it.

question: Alisson controls [Quickening Licid], [March of the Machines], and [Mycosynth Lattice] that entered the battlefield in that order. They activate Quickening Licid's ability targeting itself. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: Quickening Licid ends up in Alisson's graveyard. The ability resolves, Quickening Licid loses that activated ability and becomes an Aura enchantment with enchant creature — but Mycosynth Lattice makes that Aura an artifact, and March of the Machines then makes each noncreature artifact into an artifact creature, so the Aura is itself a creature. An Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything, so it's unattached the next time state-based actions are checked and then immediately put into its owner's graveyard as a second state-based action [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3].

Why the layers work out that way: characteristics are recalculated continuously starting from the actual object and applying continuous effects in layers [613.1a], with the type-changing part of the Licid's effect and Mycosynth Lattice's/March of the Machines's type-changing effects all applying in the type layer and power/toughness setting later [613.6]. So there is never a moment where the Licid is an Aura that is not also an artifact creature.

Targeting itself: assuming Quickening Licid was a legal target for its own ability when activated (it was a creature at that time), it is still the target on resolution, but the attachment simply can't happen/can't persist because an Aura that's a creature can't enchant anything [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3].

About the "You may pay {W} to end this effect" clause: paying it would turn Quickening Licid back into a normal creature and it would survive [Quickening Licid ruling #1 shows paying that cost undoes its enchantment status]. However, state-based actions are checked before any player receives priority after the ability resolves, so Alisson has no window to pay {W} after the ability resolves — the card is unattached and put into the graveyard first.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of opponents; the result is the same at a two-player or larger table (opposing players make no choices in this sequence).

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant is 4/4 (and an Artifact Creature — Shapeshifter Zombie Elemental).

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has that ability on the battlefield, the zone it's leaving, so the ability works and its three +1/+1 counters come with it into exile [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. Counters that adjust power and toughness still apply in zones other than the battlefield, so the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is a 4/4 in exile [122.1a], [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2].

Duplicant's static ability then says it has the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it. That's a layer 7b effect setting Duplicant's base power and toughness (its printed 2/4 is overwritten), and it also gives Duplicant Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's creature types while keeping Shapeshifter [Duplicant ruling #0], [613.1g], [613.4a]. Since the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card's power and toughness are 4/4, Duplicant is 4/4.

Note on Duplicant ruling #2: that ruling excludes *abilities* that add or subtract power and toughness (like Death's Shadow's) from applying in exile — counters are not abilities, they're markers that modify the object's characteristics directly [122.1a], so they do count here. The ability is also continuously updated, so if those counters ever ceased to exist (for example, if the card changed zones again in a way that dropped them), Duplicant's power and toughness would update accordingly [Duplicant ruling #3].

Anything that later modifies Duplicant's own power and toughness (its own counters, pump spells) still applies on top of the 4/4 base [Duplicant ruling #0]. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players — it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can legally target Pristine Angel with Murder, and Murder will destroy it.

Why: Pristine Angel's own text gives it protection from artifacts and from each color only "as long as this creature is untapped." While Pristine Angel was tapped it had no protection at all, but Cephalid Snitch's ability still resolved and applied its continuous effect: Pristine Angel loses protection from black until end of turn. That effect isn't a one-shot "strip what's there now" — it's a continuous effect lasting until end of turn, applied along with all other continuous effects each time the game recalculates Pristine Angel's characteristics (see rules 613.11 and 608.2c on following the instruction as written). So when Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from each other color, but the Cephalid Snitch effect keeps removing protection from black for the rest of the turn.

Because Pristine Angel has no protection from black, it's a legal target for Murder (a black instant), and it remains a legal target on resolution (608.2b), so it is destroyed. Note also that untapping Pristine Angel after it was declared as an attacker doesn't remove it from combat, and neither does tapping it (506.4b) — that's irrelevant to legality here, just to combat.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved before Pristine Angel untapped, as stated. If instead Pristine Angel had already untapped before Cephalid Snitch's ability was activated, Pristine Angel would have protection from blue at that moment; whether Cephalid Snitch's ability (from a blue source Nico controls) could target it would then depend on protection from blue, and Nico could not target it. Either way, once the Cephalid Snitch effect is in place, Murder works.

Multiplayer: this works the same with two players or more; nothing here depends on player count. Nico targeting Abel's Pristine Angel does count as committing a crime (700.13, Crime), which matters only if some other card cares about crimes.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment “Equipped creature has flying.” A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with “Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.” The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of Flight’s timestamp because it is later than Colossus Hammer’s timestamp. If Colossus Hammer becomes attached to a creature, both of its abilities receive new timestamps (see rule 613.7e), but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands taps for white mana only ({W}). It is a Plains.

Why: both Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") and Magus of the Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") are continuous type-changing effects applied in layer 4 (subtype-changing). Normally Conversion, with the earlier timestamp, would apply first. But there's a dependency: applying Magus of the Moon changes what Conversion applies to (Badlands, a nonbasic land, becomes a Mountain), so Conversion is applied after Magus of the Moon.

Step by step:
1. Magus of the Moon: Badlands is nonbasic, so its subtypes are set to just Mountain. Per CR 305.7 it loses its old land types (Swamp and Mountain from its printed type line) and the abilities generated from them, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #4).
2. Conversion: Badlands is now a Mountain, so Conversion sets its type to Plains. Again per CR 305.7 it loses the Mountain type and the red mana ability, and gains "{T}: Add {W}" (CR 305.6 — any land with the Plains subtype has "{T}: Add {W}").

So Badlands ends up as a nonbasic land with the single land type Plains and exactly one mana ability: {T}: Add {W}. No black, no red. Note Magus of the Moon doesn't change names or supertypes (Magus of the Moon ruling #1), and Conversion doesn't touch the snow supertype (Conversion ruling #1) — Badlands is still named Badlands and is still nonbasic.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste), and is a -5/1 creature.

Why: Fleetfeather Sandals's "Equipped creature has flying and haste" and Tightening Coils's "loses flying" both apply in layer 6 (ability-adding and ability-removing effects) [613.1f]. Neither depends on the other, so they're applied in timestamp order, and the later one wins [613.9]. An Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object [613.7e], and a continuous effect from a static ability takes the timestamp of the object it's on (or later) [613.7a]. So when Adriel re-attaches Fleetfeather Sandals with its equip ability, the Sandals' granted-flying effect gets a fresh timestamp later than Tightening Coils, and flying sticks. This matches [Tightening Coils ruling #0]: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Tightening Coils is still on Wandering Ones and its -6/-0 still applies in layer 7c, so Wandering Ones is 1-6 = -5/1 (a negative power is treated as 0 for damage purposes; it doesn't die from negative power, only from 0 or less toughness).

Note the re-equip is legal and meaningful even though Fleetfeather Sandals was already attached to Wandering Ones — attaching it again is what refreshes the timestamp [613.7e], and the equip ability targets a creature you control [Fleetfeather Sandals]. Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on how many opponents are at the table.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger ends up as a colorless 2/2 Artifact Creature — Equipment named Soldevi Digger, with no abilities at all.

How it gets there, layer by layer (CR 613.1a, 613.6, 613.7):

- Layer 4 (types): Bludgeon Brawl has the earlier timestamp, and Soldevi Digger qualified as a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact when Bludgeon Brawl began applying, so Soldevi Digger gains the Equipment subtype. Then Titania's Song (later timestamp) makes it an artifact creature. Note that once Bludgeon Brawl's effect started applying to Soldevi Digger, it keeps applying in every layer even though Soldevi Digger is now an Equipment and a creature (CR 613.6). Result: Artifact Creature — Equipment.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Bludgeon Brawl first grants "equip {2}" and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (X = Soldevi Digger's mana value, 2 — that's {2} generic in the equip cost). Then Titania's Song, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities. That strips both Soldevi Digger's printed "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" and the two abilities Bludgeon Brawl just granted. Result: no abilities.
- Layer 7b (P/T setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2}, so its mana value is 2 — it's a 2/2. Bludgeon Brawl's +X/+0 doesn't apply here; that's an ability the Equipment would grant to a creature it's attached to, and it no longer has that ability anyway.
- Color: unchanged. Soldevi Digger's mana cost {2} is entirely generic, so it has no colored mana symbols and is colorless (CR 105.2). Its mana cost stays {2} and its name stays Soldevi Digger (CR 109.3).

No dependency applies between Bludgeon Brawl and Titania's Song here — applying either doesn't change what the other does or what it applies to (CR 613.8), so plain timestamp order governs.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield before Titania's Song resolved, as stated. If Titania's Song had resolved first and Bludgeon Brawl entered afterward, Bludgeon Brawl would have the later timestamp — Soldevi Digger would still be a 2/2 artifact creature Equipment, but it would then have equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0," since the ability-granting effect would apply after the ability-removal effect in layer 6.

Also note Titania's Song's own text: "If this enchantment leaves the battlefield, this effect continues until end of turn" — that card text overrides the normal expectation that the effect ends when the source leaves.

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Wayward Angel becomes a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities (still named Wayward Angel, controlled by Ariah), for the rest of the turn.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1g, 613.7):
- Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes it a Frog — it loses Angel and Horror, remaining a Creature — Frog.
- Layer 5 (color): the threshold ability (earlier timestamp) makes it black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0) — then Turn to Frog (later timestamp) makes it blue. Net: blue only.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the threshold ability applies first (granting trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger), then Turn to Frog removes all abilities, including flying, vigilance, the threshold ability itself, and everything it granted. Net: no abilities.
- Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 (CR 613.4b; Turn to Frog ruling #0 — it overwrites earlier setting effects).
- Layer 7c: here's the catch — because the threshold ability already began applying in layer 5 before it was removed in layer 6, its +3/+3 still applies in layer 7c (CR 613.6 as reflected in the layer ordering; compare Turn to Frog ruling #4, where a God's type-changing ability applies even though the same spell removes it). So 1/1 + 3/+3 = 4/4.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ariah has seven or more cards in the graveyard both when Turn to Frog resolves and while you're checking characteristics. If the graveyard drops below seven afterward, the threshold ability is no longer generating any effect (and it's been removed anyway), so Wayward Angel would just be a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities.

Nothing here depends on the player count: the same result holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Wayward Angel is affected and control doesn't change.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Afterwards, face-up Wayward Angel is a 4/4 black Frog creature with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature." It has no flying and no vigilance, and it is black only (not white, not blue).

Why:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities ([708.2a], [708.2], [613.2b]); those were its copiable values. Turn to Frog resolving on it applied normally to that face-down object.

2. Turning it face up doesn't remove Turn to Frog's effect: as a face-down permanent is turned face up its copiable values revert to Wayward Angel's normal printed values, but any effects already applied to it still apply ([708.8], [708.10]). So now Turn to Frog's effect is applied on top of a real 4/4 white Angel Horror with flying, vigilance, and threshold, with 7 cards in Ariella's graveyard.

3. Layering ([613.1], [613.1g], [613.7]) — Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp; the threshold ability only becomes an ability of the object when it's turned face up, so its effect has the later timestamp:
   - Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes it a Frog, wiping Angel Horror. It keeps the Creature card type ([Turn to Frog ruling #1]).
   - Layer 5 (color): Turn to Frog makes it blue, then threshold (later timestamp) makes it black — and black only, not white-and-black ([Wayward Angel ruling #0]).
   - Layer 6 (abilities): Turn to Frog removes all abilities (killing flying, vigilance, and the threshold ability itself). But because the threshold effect had already started applying in layer 5, CR 613.6 says it continues to apply in every later layer even though the ability generating it is gone — so it still grants trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger at its later timestamp. (Same principle as [Turn to Frog ruling #4], where a God's type-changing ability applies before the effect removing it.)
   - Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base P/T to 1/1 ([Turn to Frog ruling #0]); layer 7c: threshold's +3/+3 still applies, giving 4/4.

4. Anything Wayward Angel gains after Turn to Frog resolved it keeps ([Turn to Frog ruling #3]). Note also that turning it face up doesn't trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities ([708.8]).

Timing assumption: I assumed Turn to Frog fully resolved before Ariella turned it face up, as stated. If instead it were turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved after, Turn to Frog would have the later timestamp: it would then be a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities at all (threshold's layer-5/6/7 effects all being overwritten or removed by the later effect).

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret. It ends up as a legendary land creature — Swamp Ferret (Swamp is a land type, Ferret its lone creature type), 6/4 and green.

How it gets there, layer by layer (CR 613 type/subtype layer, then color, then power/toughness):

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a Swamp [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0]. Note it's a Swamp only while on the battlefield [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #2].
2. Kormus Bell then makes all Swamps 1/1 black creatures that are still lands, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth becomes a land creature — it has both card types at once [Kormus Bell ruling #0], [205.2b], [205.1b].
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]. Because "[creature type] creature" effects replace existing creature types, at this point its creature type is Elemental (it keeps Swamp, which is a land type, per [205.3c] and [205.4b] — Legendary is likewise retained).
4. Conspiracy makes creatures Ahmad controls the chosen type, Ferret, and they lose all their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4], [Conspiracy ruling #1]. Even though Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, it's applied last in that layer: it applies only to creatures, and Kormus Bell and Vastwood Zendikon are what make Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature at all, so Conspiracy depends on them.

Result: card types land + creature; supertype Legendary; land type Swamp; creature type Ferret only (Elemental is gone); color green (Vastwood Zendikon's color-setting is later than Kormus Bell's black); 6/4 (Vastwood Zendikon's set P/T is later than Kormus Bell's 1/1). Ferret is a legal choice for Conspiracy since it's on the creature type list [205.3m]; "Legend" would not be [Conspiracy ruling #2].

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — Conspiracy only cares about creatures Ahmad controls, and Kormus Bell/Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth affect all Swamps/lands regardless of table size.

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
Raugrin Triome ends up with just one land type: Mountain. It taps only for {R}.

Why: both Prismatic Omen and Blood Moon are type-changing continuous effects, so they're applied in layer 4 in timestamp order. Prismatic Omen was already on the battlefield, so it applies first, making Raugrin Triome all five basic land types (Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest) in addition to its printed Island Mountain Plains [Prismatic Omen ruling #0]. Blood Moon then resolves with a later timestamp and says nonbasic lands "are Mountains," which sets the land type rather than adding to it — Raugrin Triome loses every other land type and the abilities that came with them, and has only Mountain [Blood Moon ruling #2]. Raugrin Triome is still nonbasic (it has no "basic" supertype), so Blood Moon does apply to it [Nonbasic Land], and neither effect changes its name or supertypes [Blood Moon ruling #1] [Prismatic Omen ruling #1].

Because it has the basic land type Mountain, Raugrin Triome has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" and nothing else mana-wise [305.6] [Mountain]. Its printed cycling {3} ability is not a land-type-granted ability, but Blood Moon's text explicitly strips the abilities nonbasic lands had while they're on the battlefield [Blood Moon ruling #2]; cycling is only usable from hand anyway.

Timing note: I'm assuming Prismatic Omen was on the battlefield before Blood Moon resolved, as stated. If Prismatic Omen instead entered after Blood Moon, its later timestamp would apply on top and Raugrin Triome would have all five basic land types (Mountain plus Plains, Island, Swamp, Forest) and could tap for any color.

This result is the same regardless of the number of players; the controllers of Prismatic Omen and Blood Moon being different players doesn't affect layer ordering — only timestamps do.

question: Ariel controls [Frostboil Snarl] and [Blood Moon]. They cast [Prismatic Omen]. After it resolves, what land types does Frostboil Snarl have?
answer:
Frostboil Snarl ends up with all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest 
}or rather — Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest — and it taps for any color.

How it gets there (layer 4, subtype-changing effects, applied in timestamp order):
1. Blood Moon (older timestamp) sets Frostboil Snarl's subtype to Mountain, because Frostboil Snarl is a nonbasic land — it has no "basic" supertype [205.4c]. Under CR 305.7, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and all abilities from its rules text, so Frostboil Snarl loses its enters-tapped ability and its printed "{T}: Add {U} or {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2]. It gains the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain [305.6].
2. Prismatic Omen (newer timestamp) then makes lands Ariel controls every basic land type in addition to their other types. That's an additive effect, so Frostboil Snarl keeps Mountain and gains Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest [305.7, Prismatic Omen ruling #0].

Resulting abilities: the intrinsic mana ability of each basic land type — "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6]. Note each activation taps it, so it makes one mana of a color of Ariel's choice.

Other notes: neither effect touches supertypes or names, so Frostboil Snarl is still a nonbasic land and still named Frostboil Snarl [Blood Moon ruling #1, Prismatic Omen ruling #1, 205.4c]. Frostboil Snarl's own printed abilities stay gone — Blood Moon's ability-removal applies in layer 6 regardless of the later subtype addition. Prismatic Omen only affects lands Ariel controls; Blood Moon affects every nonbasic land on the battlefield, so in a multiplayer game other players' nonbasic lands are Mountains only, while this answer is unchanged for Ariel's own lands whether there are two players or more.

question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Short answer: Winged Temple of Orazca definitely loses its printed "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability, and it can tap only for the basic-land-type mana it ends up having — either {R} only, or all five colors {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, depending on which of Blood Moon or Prismatic Omen applies later in layer 4. Because Karn Liberated's −14 puts Blood Moon, Prismatic Omen, and Winged Temple of Orazca onto the battlefield simultaneously, the two enchantments have the same timestamp, and the rules provided here contain no tiebreaker for that, so I can't state one single result as certain.

Why:
- Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic (Legendary) land, so Blood Moon sets its subtype to Mountain and, per Blood Moon ruling #2, strips its other land types and its printed abilities, giving it "{T}: Add {R}." That kills both the any-color mana ability and the {1}{G}{U}, {T} pump ability.
- Prismatic Omen says lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types; per Prismatic Omen ruling #0 the land then has Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest and the mana ability of each.
- Any land with a basic land type has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add [that color]" even with no text box ([305.6], [Plains], [Mountain], [107.4a]) — so the mana abilities follow from the types, which is why Blood Moon's ability-wipe doesn't stop the type-granted mana abilities.

The two outcomes (I ran both layer orders):
1. If Prismatic Omen's type-setting applies after Blood Moon's: subtypes are Mountain, Plains, Island, Swamp, Forest → taps for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one mana of your choice among those).
2. If Blood Moon's applies after Prismatic Omen's: subtypes are just Mountain → taps for {R} only.

Either way the printed "any color" ability and the {1}{G}{U}, {T} ability are gone, and note {C} is never available here — colorless is not a color ([105.1], [105.4], [Colorless]).

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players; these are Adan's own permanents and no rule provided here makes the outcome depend on the number of opponents.

What's missing from the provided context: the timestamp/tiebreak rule (CR 613.7 family) for permanents entering the battlefield simultaneously. If a later-applied Prismatic Omen is chosen, you get all five colors; otherwise just red.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a **Land Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island**, and it's a green 1/1.

How it gets there (all in layer 4 for types/subtypes):

1. **Arcane Adaptation** (naming Saproling) makes every creature Apollo controls that type in addition to its others, so Realmwright becomes a Vedalken Wizard Saproling. Saproling is a legal creature type to name (Arcane Adaptation ruling #1, CR 205.3m).
2. **Life and Limb** then sees Realmwright as a Saproling, so it applies: Realmwright becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types. It keeps the creature type and gains the land card type, plus subtypes Saproling and Forest. Per CR 205.1b, "in addition to their other types" means all prior card types and subtypes are retained. Per Life and Limb ruling #3, each subtype stays correlated to the right card type: Forest is a land type only, Saproling is a creature type only (CR 205.3c, 205.3i, 205.3m).
3. **Realmwright's own** static ability ("Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types," naming Island) now applies to Realmwright itself, because Life and Limb made it a land. Even though Realmwright has the earliest timestamp, its effect is applied *after* Life and Limb's: applying Life and Limb changes what Realmwright's effect applies to, so Realmwright's effect is dependent on it (dependency, not timestamp, sets the order). Realmwright therefore also gains the land type Island. Island is a basic land type, a legal choice (Realmwright ruling #1, CR 305.6).

Consequences: as a land with the basic land types Forest and Island, Realmwright has the intrinsic mana abilities "{T}: Add {G}" and "{T}: Add {U}" (CR 305.6) — though as a creature it's subject to summoning sickness for tapping. In layer 5 Life and Limb sets its color to green (it is no longer blue), and in layer 7b its power and toughness are set to 1/1. It has no supertypes, and none are added or removed (CR 205.4b).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since all three permanents only affect permanents Apollo controls or all Forests/Saprolings.

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token will be legendary once it's on the battlefield, and the legend rule will then force Ainsley to keep only one of the two Awoken Demons.

Why: Helm of the Host's copy effect says the token "isn't legendary," so as a copiable value the token starts out non-legendary (Helm of the Host ruling #3). But Leyline of Singularity is a separate continuous static effect that says "All nonland permanents are legendary," and it applies to the token as soon as the token is on the battlefield, independent of copy effects. Adding the legendary supertype doesn't remove the token's other supertypes or change its types (Leyline of Singularity ruling #0, [205.4b]).

Consequence: the token is a copy of Awoken Demon, so it has the name Awoken Demon, the same as the original creature Ainsley controls. Because Leyline of Singularity makes both the token and the original Awoken Demon legendary, and both are controlled by Ainsley with the same name, the legend rule state-based action applies: Ainsley chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard ([704.5j], [205.4d]). Leyline of Singularity ruling #2 confirms this outcome specifically for tokens. If Ainsley keeps the token, it has haste from Helm of the Host; if Ainsley keeps the original Awoken Demon, the token goes to the graveyard and then ceases to exist. Either way Helm of the Host stays attached to whichever creature it was equipped to (it doesn't attach to the token).

Note that with Leyline of Singularity out, Helm of the Host's "isn't legendary" exception is effectively neutralized — the exception normally exists precisely to dodge the legend rule (Helm of the Host ruling #3), but Leyline of Singularity re-applies the supertype afterward.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Leyline of Singularity and the legend rule both apply per-player, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.
