question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
Direct answer: the two basic lands (Snow-Covered Island and Mountain) end up with all five basic land types and all five mana abilities; the two nonbasic lands (Study Hall and Dryad Arbor) end up as plain Mountains that only tap for {R} (Dryad Arbor also stays a green 1/1 Dryad creature).

Both effects are type-changing effects applied in layer 4, in timestamp order: Dryad of the Ilysian Grove first, then Blood Moon (newer). Neither depends on the other — Blood Moon keys off the "basic" supertype, and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove doesn't change supertypes [205.4c], [Blood Moon ruling #1].

- Snow-Covered Island: Basic Snow Land — Island Plains Swamp Mountain Forest. Blood Moon doesn't touch it (it's basic). It has "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", and "{T}: Add {G}" as intrinsic abilities [305.6], [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0]. Snow is a supertype with no meaning by itself [205.4g], [Snow-Covered Island ruling #0].
- Mountain: Basic Land — Mountain Plains Island Swamp Forest, likewise tapping for any of the five colors [305.6].
- Study Hall: nonbasic, so Blood Moon (later timestamp) overwrites its land types: Land — Mountain, with only "{T}: Add {R}". It loses "{T}: Add {C}" and its "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color…" ability, and it loses the five types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove gave it [Blood Moon ruling #2], [305.6].
- Dryad Arbor: nonbasic (no "basic" supertype despite having Forest) [205.4c]. It becomes Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, a green 1/1 with only "{T}: Add {R}". Blood Moon only replaces its land types; the creature type Dryad and creature card type remain, and its color comes from its color indicator, not from a type-changing effect [205.3c], [Dryad Arbor ruling #0], [Dryad Arbor ruling #2], [Dryad Arbor ruling #3]. Note Dryad Arbor is also still subject to summoning sickness.

Names and supertypes are untouched throughout — nothing becomes named "Mountain" and nothing becomes basic [Blood Moon ruling #1].

Timing note: I assume Dryad of the Ilysian Grove was already on the battlefield when Blood Moon resolved (as stated). If Blood Moon were the older permanent and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered afterward, the timestamps flip and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove would apply last, giving Study Hall and Dryad Arbor all five basic land types (and all five mana abilities) on top of Blood Moon's Mountain.

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with player count — Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands on the battlefield regardless of controller, while Dryad of the Ilysian Grove only affects lands Addison controls.

question: Angelina has seven cards in their hand, controls [Trusted Advisor], and casts [Null Profusion]. After Angelina discards at the end of the turn, how many cards should they have in their hand?
answer:
Angelina ends up with two cards in hand.

Because Null Profusion entered the battlefield after Trusted Advisor, its effect is applied later in timestamp order and simply sets Angelina's maximum hand size to two, overwriting the earlier result [Trusted Advisor ruling #0], [Null Profusion ruling #3]. Trusted Advisor's "+2" was applied first (7 + 2 = 9), then Null Profusion's "Your maximum hand size is two" sets the value flatly to 2. Card text like this overrides the normal default of seven [402.2].

Maximum hand size is the number a player must discard down to during their cleanup step: immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand has more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard enough cards to reduce it to that number, as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1], [703.4n], [Maximum Hand Size].

Timing note: I'm assuming Null Profusion resolved and was on the battlefield before Angelina's cleanup step, and that the seven cards counted included Null Profusion itself (so six remain after casting it) — either way the discard brings the hand to two. If Null Profusion somehow were not on the battlefield at cleanup (countered, destroyed, etc.), only Trusted Advisor would apply and Angelina's maximum hand size would be nine, so no discard would happen. Also note this discard only occurs during Angelina's own cleanup step, i.e., on Angelina's turn.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

answer_gold: Two. Trusted Advisor adds two to the maximum hand size (making it nine), and Null Profusion then sets the maximum hand to two.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Nico's Thespian's Stage is a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and only one ability: "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Alayna's Thespian's Stage becomes a full, unmolested copy of Temple of Triumph that also keeps a Thespian's Stage copy ability.

Nico's Stage in detail: the copy effect from its own ability is applied in layer 1 and has no duration, so its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph plus the exception ability "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" (CR 707.2, 707.9a, 613.1a, 613.2a/613.2c, Thespian's Stage ruling #0). Its name is therefore Temple of Triumph, so Alpine Moon's static effect applies to it (Nico is Alayna's opponent): in layer 4 it loses all land types (Temple of Triumph has none printed anyway) and in layer 6 it loses all abilities -- including the granted Thespian's Stage copy ability and the enters-tapped/scry/mana abilities -- then gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" from that same Alpine Moon effect (CR 613.6, 613.7, 613.8). It's still a land, and Alpine Moon doesn't touch card types or supertypes (Alpine Moon ruling #1). It also didn't untap or re-enter (Thespian's Stage rulings #1 and #2).

Alayna's Stage in detail: Alpine Moon only hits lands *your opponents* control, so Alayna's own land is unaffected by it even though its name is Temple of Triumph. When Alayna's Stage copies Nico's Stage (the permanent named Temple of Triumph), it copies copiable values only -- Alpine Moon's ability-removal is a layer 6 effect, not copiable, so it isn't copied (CR 707.2). So Alayna's Stage is a land named Temple of Triumph with "This land enters tapped," "When this land enters, scry 1," "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and the Thespian's Stage copy ability (present from Nico's copy exception and re-added by Alayna's own "except it has this ability"; duplicates are redundant, CR 707.9a). The enters-tapped and scry abilities do nothing now, since it was already on the battlefield (Thespian's Stage ruling #1), and it doesn't untap (ruling #2).

Assumption: Alayna's activation targeted Nico's Stage (the only permanent named Temple of Triumph). If she instead targeted some genuine Temple of Triumph land she or someone else controls, the result for her Stage is identical.

Multiplayer: nothing changes structurally -- Alpine Moon hits the named lands controlled by *each* of Alpine Moon's controller's opponents, so in a bigger game every opponent's Temple of Triumph-named land is stripped the same way, while Alayna's own stays intact.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature and becomes just an enchantment. One with the Stars has the later timestamp, so its type-changing effect is applied after Kenrith's Transformation's, and the later effect wins where they conflict (rule 613.9, applied continuously per rule 613.5).

Step by step:
- Kenrith's Transformation makes Thraben Purebloods lose all abilities and be a green Elk creature with base power/toughness 3/3, overwriting its colors and creature types (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3).
- One with the Stars then makes Thraben Purebloods an enchantment and makes it lose all other card types. Because the Elk creature type is a subtype tied to the creature card type it just lost, Thraben Purebloods loses the Elk subtype too (One with the Stars ruling #2). Any supertypes would be kept.
- Thraben Purebloods is still green, and the 3/3 base power/toughness setting effect from Kenrith's Transformation still technically applies, but power and toughness are meaningless while it isn't a creature. It also still has no abilities (Kenrith's Transformation), except that abilities gained after Kenrith's Transformation became attached would be kept (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #6).

One caveat: Kenrith's Transformation says "Enchant creature," and Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature, so Kenrith's Transformation is no longer legally attached (rule 702.5c requires the enchanted object to match all enchant abilities). The provided rules don't include the state-based action that handles an Aura attached to an illegal object, so I can't cite what happens to it from this context. If Kenrith's Transformation does leave the battlefield, its effects end and Thraben Purebloods reverts to being a white Dog with its own printed characteristics — but One with the Stars keeps it an enchantment and not a creature (One with the Stars ruling #1 shows that effect persists even when the creature-ness came from elsewhere).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The resulting mutated permanent is a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types other than creature, no mana cost, and no subtypes — because a merged permanent takes its other characteristics from its topmost component, and here the topmost component is the face-down manifested card ([730.2a], [702.140e]). On top of that, it has the abilities of every component, so it has Trumpeting Gnarr's ability "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" ([702.140e]), and that ability triggers on this very mutation, giving Avery a 3/3 green Beast token ([702.140d]).

How it got there: Trumpeting Gnarr was cast for its mutate cost {3}{G/U}{G/U} (each {G/U} paid with either one green or one blue mana; the {3} is generic), making it a mutating creature spell targeting a non-Human creature Avery owns — the face-down manifest qualifies, since a face-down creature has no creature types and so isn't Human ([702.140a], [707.3]). As it resolved it did not enter the battlefield; it merged with the manifested creature, and Avery chose to put it underneath ([702.140c], [608.3d], [730.2a]). Merging is a copiable effect applied in layer 1a ([613.2], [613.2a]).

Practical notes: the permanent is still face down and still has "phased in / face down" status ([110.5]), so Avery may later turn it face up for its mana cost if the manifested card is a creature card (per Soul Summons); if it's turned face up, that face-up card's characteristics become the topmost component's characteristics, while the Trumpeting Gnarr ability underneath is retained. Had Avery instead put Trumpeting Gnarr on top, the permanent would be a 3/3 green Beast named Trumpeting Gnarr with that same mutate trigger. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon still has flying, and it's an 8/8.

Why: everything here is sorted in layer 6 (ability adding/removing, including keyword counters) by timestamp (CR 613.1, 613.1f, 613.7a). In order:
1. Spontaneous Flight #1 puts a flying counter on Mist Dragon — Mist Dragon has flying (and +2/+2 in layer 7c).
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying" — that removal has a later timestamp, so it beats the first counter and Mist Dragon has no flying (CR 113.10b, 113.10c, 613.9). Note the removal effect lasts indefinitely; it does not remove the counter itself, it just out-timestamps it.
3. Spontaneous Flight #2 puts a second flying counter on Mist Dragon, with the latest timestamp of all three effects. Most recent wins, so Mist Dragon has flying again (and is now 8/8 from the two +2/+2 effects).
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter. One flying counter remains. Since the two flying counters are identical objects on the permanent and the surviving one is treated as the still-existing later counter, its timestamp is still later than the "loses flying" activation, so Mist Dragon keeps flying.

Assumption on the ambiguous point: which of the two indistinguishable flying counters Hex Parasite "removed." Counters of the same kind aren't tracked separately, so the remaining flying counter is just "a flying counter now on Mist Dragon," post-dating the lose-flying effect. If instead you insisted the surviving counter were the pre-lose-flying one, the "{0}: loses flying" effect would be the latest layer-6 effect and Mist Dragon would not have flying — but there's no rules basis for distinguishing the counters that way. Also note Hex Parasite only gets +1/+0 for counters actually removed (Hex Parasite ruling #0), so it gets +1/+0 here.

If April wants Mist Dragon to lose flying, she can simply activate "{0}: This creature loses flying" again for a fresh, latest timestamp. Nothing here depends on the number of players; it's a one-sided sequence of April's own actions, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games (in multiplayer, other players holding removal-of-flying effects could of course respond, and per CR 732.3 the player acting last in such a back-and-forth determines the final state).

question: Avery casts [Vulpikeet] for its mutate cost, mutating under a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. They then cast [Rootborn Defenses], choosing to populate the merged permanent. What happens?
answer:
Avery can populate the merged permanent, because its topmost component is the Goblin creature token, so the merged permanent is a creature token Avery controls. The new token is a copy of that merged permanent's copiable characteristics — a 1/1 red Goblin with flying and "Whenever this creature mutates, put a +1/+1 counter on it" — and it, along with Avery's other creatures at that moment, gains indestructible until end of turn.

Details:

- Mutate: casting Vulpikeet for its mutate cost makes it a mutating creature spell targeting a non-Human creature Avery owns [702.140a]. On resolution Vulpikeet doesn't enter the battlefield separately; it merges with the Goblin token into one object represented by more than one card/token, and Avery chose to put Vulpikeet on the bottom [702.140c, 730.1, 608.3d]. The mutated permanent has all abilities of both components (so it has flying and Vulpikeet's mutate trigger), but all its other characteristics — name, types, colors, power/toughness — come from the topmost component, the 1/1 red Goblin token [702.140e]. Vulpikeet's own "whenever this creature mutates" ability triggered and put a +1/+1 counter on it [702.140d], making it 2/2 on the battlefield.
- Populate: to populate you choose a creature token you control and create a token that's a copy of it [701.36a]. Since the merged permanent's characteristics are those of the Goblin token, it qualifies as a creature token Avery controls and is a legal choice.
- What the copy looks like: characteristic changes from merging an object with a permanent are copiable effects applied in layer 1a [613.2a], so the copy takes the merged permanent's copiable values: a 1/1 red Goblin creature token with flying and the mutate-triggered ability. It is a single new token, not a merged pile — Vulpikeet itself stays where it is, under the original. Non-copiable things like the +1/+1 counter and any temporary pumps aren't copied, so the new token is 1/1.
- Indestructible: Rootborn Defenses grants indestructible until end of turn to the creatures Avery controls after populating, including the freshly created token, but not to creatures Avery comes to control later in the turn [Rootborn Defenses ruling #0]. That includes the merged permanent itself.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since populate and Rootborn Defenses only involve Avery's own creatures.

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan is a -1/1 (power -1, toughness 1) while enchanted by Mystic Subdual.

Why: Fiend Artisan is printed 1/1, and its "gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is an ordinary static ability that would apply in layer 7c ([613.4c]), not a characteristic-defining ability that sets power/toughness (compare [604.3], [208.2a] — Fiend Artisan's printed box is 1/1, not */*). Continuous effects apply in layer order ([613.1g], [302.4c]).

- Layer 6 (ability-changing): Mystic Subdual makes Fiend Artisan lose all abilities, so the +1/+1-per-creature-card ability is gone before layer 7 is reached.
- Layer 7c: Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 applies. Fiend Artisan's own pump doesn't apply at all, because the ability generating it was removed in layer 6 and had never started applying in an earlier layer ([613.6] only protects effects that already began applying).

So 1/1 - 2/-0 = -1/1. Power below 0 is simply treated as 0 for damage-dealing purposes; the four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard are irrelevant while the Aura is attached (and Fiend Artisan's boost only ever works on the battlefield anyway — [Fiend Artisan ruling #2]).

Note the contrast drawn by [Mystic Subdual ruling #1]: that ruling covers creatures printed */* whose power/toughness comes from a characteristic-defining ability — those become 0/0 base and then -2/0. Fiend Artisan is not such a card; its 1/1 is printed, so the printed 1/1 survives and only the +4/+4 is lost.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — nothing here involves defending players or opponents' turns, so it's identical in two-player and multiplayer games. Timing note: I'm assuming Mystic Subdual is already attached and resolved. If you check Fiend Artisan's size before Mystic Subdual resolves, it's 5/5 (1/1 plus +4/+4 for the four creature cards).

question: Ari controls [Xathrid Gorgon]. Neriah controls a [Hexavus] and [Stonehewer Giant]. Ari activates Xathrid Gorgon to put a petrification counter on Stonehewer Giant which Neriah removes with Hexavus. Can Neriah activate Stonehewer Giant's activated ability?
answer:
No. Neriah still can't activate Stonehewer Giant's {1}{W}, {T} ability, even after removing the petrification counter with Hexavus's "{1}, Remove a counter from another creature you control" ability.

Xathrid Gorgon's ability creates a continuous effect that doesn't depend on the petrification counter remaining on the creature. Per [Xathrid Gorgon ruling #0], if that counter is removed, the affected creature (here Stonehewer Giant) remains a colorless artifact with defender, and its activated abilities still can't be activated. The counter is just a marker/reminder, not the source of the effect.

Since an effect says Stonehewer Giant's activated abilities can't be activated, Neriah can't even begin to activate the search-for-Equipment ability ([602.5]), and a "can't" effect takes precedence over the general permission that a player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority ([101.2a], [117.1b]).

Removing the counter with Hexavus is still legal and does put a +1/+1 counter on Hexavus — it just doesn't undo the petrification. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the same answer applies at a two-player or multiplayer table (Neriah simply must be within range of influence to activate anything at all, [801.6]).

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The mutated creature will be 1/1.

Why: mutate makes one permanent — a mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it, and its other characteristics (name, P/T, colors, types) come from the topmost card or token [702.140e]. With Glowstone Recluse on top, the copiable/base P/T is 2/3.

Then Nico's Humility applies as a continuous effect through the layer system [613.1, 302.4c]:
- Layer 6: the mutated permanent loses all abilities (Reach and the mutate trigger included).
- Layer 7b: Humility sets its base power and toughness to 1/1 — this is a "set" effect, applied in sublayer 7b [613.4b, 208.4a, Base Power, Base Toughness].

No layer 7c modifiers apply, because the "Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it" ability is removed by Humility in layer 6 before/at the time the mutation occurs — Humility's effect applies continuously and automatically [613.5], so on the battlefield the permanent never has that triggered ability and no +1/+1 counters are created. (Had counters somehow already been on the creature, they would still apply in layer 7c on top of the 1/1, per the Gray Ogre example in [613.5, 613.4c].) Maritime Guard's 1/3 is irrelevant once it's the under-card: only its abilities carry over, and those are stripped too.

Timestamp note: Humility is already on the battlefield here, so it has the earlier timestamp; but since only one 7b effect exists (Humility's), timestamp order [613.7] doesn't change anything — the answer is 1/1 either way. If some other set-P/T effect were involved, the Humility/Opalescence rulings show timestamps would matter [Humility ruling #2].

Multiplayer: this doesn't change with more than two players — Humility says "all creatures," regardless of controller.

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument is still a colorless, noncreature Land named "Forgotten Monument," but its only subtype is Mountain, its only ability is "{T}: Add {R}," and it is not a Cave and has no {T}: Add {C} or Cave-granting ability. It's also not a basic land.

Why: Lizard, Connors's Curse's trigger makes Magus of the Moon lose all abilities and become a green Lizard creature with base power and toughness 4/4 (and that effect doesn't end at end of turn, per Lizard, Connors's Curse ruling #0). But losing abilities in layer 6 does not undo what Magus of the Moon's ability already did in layer 4. Type-changing effects (layer 4) are applied before ability-adding/removing effects (layer 6), regardless of the order the effects started, and once an effect starts to apply in one layer it keeps applying in every other applicable layer even if the ability generating it is removed (CR 613.1, 613.1d, 613.1f, 613.6). Magus of the Moon ruling #0 states this outcome directly: if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it still turns nonbasic lands into Mountains.

So in layer 4, Forgotten Monument's land subtype Cave is replaced by Mountain; in layer 6 it loses its printed abilities ("{T}: Add {C}" and the Cave-granting ability) and gains the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #4). Its name and any supertypes are unaffected, and it does not become basic (Magus of the Moon ruling #1; CR 205.4b). Since it no longer grants the any-color ability, Alex's other Caves lose that granted ability too.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as the state after Lizard, Connors's Curse has fully resolved, with Magus of the Moon still on the battlefield (now a 4/4 green Lizard). If instead Magus of the Moon had left the battlefield, its effect would end entirely and Forgotten Monument would revert to a Cave with its printed abilities.

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying, and it's a 12/11.

Why: Rune of Flight enchants Colossus Hammer (an Equipment), so Rune of Flight gives Colossus Hammer the ability "Equipped creature has flying." That granted ability's timestamp is Rune of Flight's timestamp, since that's later than Colossus Hammer's own timestamp [613.7a]. Colossus Hammer's printed ability "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying" has the earlier timestamp of the two.

When Colossus Hammer becomes attached to Skeletal Snake, Colossus Hammer receives a new timestamp [613.7e], and both of its abilities (its own and the one granted by Rune of Flight) receive new timestamps — but their relative order is preserved [613.7a]. So in layer 6 (ability-adding/removing), "loses flying" applies first and "has flying" applies second; the later effect wins [613.9]. Neither depends on the other; it's pure timestamp order [613.9]. Adding and removing abilities is not governed by the "can't beats can" rule, so "loses flying" doesn't automatically trump [101.2a, 113.10].

Separately, in layer 7c, Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 still applies, making Skeletal Snake 12/11.

Order matters here: this is the case where Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer *before* Colossus Hammer was equipped, as stated. If instead Colossus Hammer were already equipped to Skeletal Snake and Rune of Flight came down afterward, the answer is the same — Rune of Flight's granted ability is still later, and Colossus Hammer's own ruling confirms that a creature gaining flying after Colossus Hammer is attached keeps flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #2]. Note this is not a "has flying as long as" ability on Skeletal Snake itself, so [Colossus Hammer ruling #1] doesn't apply.

Player count doesn't change any of this; nothing here depends on the number of opponents. Also note Rune of Flight's first clause ("As long as enchanted permanent is a creature, it has flying") does nothing, since Colossus Hammer is an Equipment artifact, not a creature.

question: Ashley equips [Colossus Hammer] to [Ogre Warrior], then enchants it with [Phantom Wings]. Does Ogre Warrior have flying?
answer:
Yes — Ogre Warrior has flying, and it's a 13/13.

Both ability-affecting effects apply in layer 6 (adding/removing abilities), so they're ordered by timestamp (613.7a, 613.7e). Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" got its timestamp when it became attached; Phantom Wings' "Enchanted creature has flying" got a later timestamp when the Aura entered attached. Neither effect depends on the other — nothing about one changes what the other applies to or does — so they simply apply in timestamp order and the later one wins (613.9). Removing flying first, then granting it, leaves Ogre Warrior with flying. This matches Colossus Hammer ruling #2: if the equipped creature gains flying after Colossus Hammer became attached, it keeps flying.

Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 applies in layer 7c regardless, so Ogre Warrior is 13/13 with flying (613.5).

If the order had been reversed — Phantom Wings first, then equipping Colossus Hammer — Colossus Hammer's effect would have the later timestamp and Ogre Warrior would be a 13/13 without flying. Note also that if Colossus Hammer is later re-attached (even to the same creature via a new attach event), it receives a new, later timestamp (613.7e) and would then strip flying.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the result is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?
answer:
Yes — Ari's Dormant Volcano is still a Mountain.

Ichthyomorphosis makes enchanted Magus of the Moon lose all abilities, but that doesn't stop Magus of the Moon's land-type change. Effects that change subtypes are applied before effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which those effects began, so Magus of the Moon continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains even after losing its abilities [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

Consequences for Dormant Volcano:
- It loses its other land types and its own abilities — so it loses "This land enters tapped," the enter-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger, and "{T}: Add {C}{R}" — and it gains the land type Mountain and the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], [305.6], [Mountain].
- Note {C} (colorless mana specifically) is no longer available from it; it only produces {R}.
- It is not a basic land and it isn't renamed "Mountain"; Magus of the Moon doesn't affect names or supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].

Also relevant: Ichthyomorphosis makes Magus of the Moon a blue Fish 0/1, but it remains a creature, so the Aura stays attached and Magus of the Moon stays on the battlefield applying its type-changing effect (it would only fall off if the enchanted permanent stopped being a creature) [Ichthyomorphosis ruling #5].

This works the same regardless of player count — Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, including those of every opponent at a multiplayer table.

question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up a 6/6 black Creature — Angel Horror with no abilities.

Walking the layers (CR 613.1f/613.1g, 613.7):

- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold ability (active, since Averie has 7+ cards in the graveyard) makes it black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0). This is where the threshold ability *starts to apply*.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Wayward Angel's own threshold ability would grant trample and the upkeep-sacrifice trigger (timestamp: when Wayward Angel entered), but Humility, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities from all creatures. Net result: no abilities at all — no flying, no vigilance, no threshold, no trample.
- Layer 7b (set P/T): Humility sets base power and toughness to 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modify P/T): Muraganda Petroglyphs checks live state here — after layer 6, Wayward Angel truly has no abilities, so it gets +2/+2 (3/3). Note Petroglyphs cares about abilities, and effects that merely set a characteristic or state a quality don't count as abilities (CR 113.12). Then Wayward Angel's threshold +3/+3 still applies: under CR 613.6, an effect that started applying in an earlier layer (layer 5, the color change) keeps applying in every later applicable layer even though Humility stripped the ability generating it in layer 6 — the same principle shown in Humility ruling #2. That brings it to 6/6.

So: 6/6, black, Creature — Angel Horror, no abilities. Order within layer 7c doesn't matter here (both are additions).

Timing assumption: Humility resolved after Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield, so Humility has the later timestamp. If Humility had somehow been on the battlefield first with Wayward Angel entering later, layer 6 would still strip everything (Humility's ability-removal applies continuously to all creatures), but in layer 7b the later effect applies last — with Humility earliest, Wayward Angel's base would still be 1/1 since no other effect sets P/T, so the result is the same 6/6.

Player count doesn't change anything here; the provided rules and cards involve no defending-player or per-opponent choices, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games ("your graveyard" is Averie's graveyard either way).

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Alexzander's Jinx makes Nico's Urza's Saga lose its chapter abilities, and since it's still a Saga, Nico must immediately sacrifice it as a state-based action.

Details:

1. Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn," so Alexzander chooses a basic land type for Urza's Saga. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes the land lose its old land type (Urza's Saga) and lose all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and copiable effects affecting it; it gains the mana ability of the chosen basic land type [305.7]. The chapter abilities (I, II, III) are printed rules-text abilities, so they're gone.

2. Land types are land subtypes; Saga is an *enchantment* subtype, and setting a land's subtype only replaces subtypes from that set (land types) [201.1a-style rule 205.1a]. So Urza's Saga is still an enchantment Saga — with no chapter abilities and two lore counters on it.

3. That situation is exactly the one covered by the Urza's Saga ruling: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed" [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. This sacrifice happens as a state-based action the next time a player would receive priority; it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to [704.5s, 714.4].

4. Abilities Urza's Saga already *gained* from chapters I and II ({T}: Add {C}, and the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability) were granted by resolved effects rather than by its own rules text, so rule 305.7 doesn't strip those [305.7, Urza's Saga ruling #5] — but that hardly matters, since Nico sacrifices the permanent right away. If Nico wants value, he should activate the Construct-token ability (if he has {2} and it's untapped) before priority passes back — practically, Alexzander casting Jinx puts the ability on the stack and Nico can respond while Jinx is still on the stack, before the type change happens.

Assumed timing: I'm reading this as Jinx resolving while Urza's Saga has two lore counters and no chapter ability of its own on the stack. If instead a chapter ability of Urza's Saga were still on the stack, the sacrifice would be delayed only in the case covered by [714.4]/[704.5s] (a Saga isn't sacrificed while it's the source of a triggered chapter ability that hasn't left the stack) — but with the chapter abilities removed, the ruling's immediate sacrifice still applies once that ability finishes resolving.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since Jinx targets a single land and the sacrifice is performed by that land's controller, Nico.

question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus ends up as an 11/11 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect (plus its own two activated abilities).

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.7, timestamp order within each layer):
- Layer 4 (types): both activations of Inkmoth Nexus make it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — and it's still a land. Applying the same effect twice changes nothing further.
- Layer 6 (abilities): first activation (timestamp 1) grants flying and infect; Colossus Hammer (timestamp 2 — an Equipment gets a new timestamp when it becomes attached, CR 613.7e) removes flying; the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus (timestamp 3) grants flying and infect again. Because that grant has the latest timestamp in layer 6, Inkmoth Nexus has flying. Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" only strips flying that exists when it's applied; it doesn't stop a later effect from granting it back.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): both Inkmoth Nexus activations set it to 1/1; the later one wins, still 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifications): Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 applies after, giving 11/11.

So the order matters: had Aaden equipped Colossus Hammer after the second activation, Colossus Hammer's ability would have the latest timestamp in layer 6 and Inkmoth Nexus would lose flying (it would still be 11/11 with infect).

Colors: nothing here changes color, so Inkmoth Nexus remains colorless (becoming an artifact doesn't grant a color). Timing assumption: all three actions resolved in the order stated, all during the same turn, so both animation effects are still active ("until end of turn").

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's identical in two-player and multiplayer games. Note also Inkmoth Nexus ruling #0/#1: it can only attack or tap for mana if Aaden has controlled it continuously since his most recent turn began.

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: the ability resolves, and the Copy Artifact permanent stops being a Dance of the Dead Aura and becomes a 6/4 Wurm named Streetbreaker Wurm, keeping only the {1}{U}{R} copy ability it granted itself. Because it never left the battlefield, Dance of the Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability is simply gone rather than triggering, so the Viashino Warrior stays on the battlefield as a plain 4/2, no longer enchanted, no longer +1/+1, and no longer barred from untapping.

Why it works:

1. Legal target: Streetbreaker Wurm is a permanent, and Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Streetbreaker Wurm is a legal target for the "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability that the Copy Artifact permanent inherited (via Mizzium Transreliquat's copiable values, which were Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus that ability — see Mizzium Transreliquat rulings #0 and #3, and 707.9b).

2. New copy effect overwrites the old one: a permanent that becomes a copy of something else takes on the new copiable values entirely; it doesn't stack the previous copy effect on top (707.3, 707.4, Mizzium Transreliquat rulings #0 and #4). So the Copy Artifact permanent loses Dance of the Dead's text, loses the "it's an enchantment in addition to its other types" modification from Copy Artifact's own entry, and loses Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' abilities. All it retains is Streetbreaker Wurm's copiable values plus the {1}{U}{R} ability, because that ability's own exception re-grants it (707.9b).

3. No leaves-the-battlefield or enters-the-battlefield triggers: becoming a copy of a different object while remaining on the battlefield doesn't cause ETB or LTB abilities to trigger (707.4). The Dance of the Dead sacrifice clause is therefore never triggered — it ceased to exist as an ability while the permanent stayed put — so the returned Viashino Warrior survives.

4. Attachment: since the permanent is no longer an Aura, it can't remain attached to Viashino Warrior; it simply becomes an unattached permanent the next time state-based actions are checked (compare Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3, which unattaches an Aura that becomes a creature).

5. It's an artifact creature: March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked, so nothing is animating noncreature artifacts, but that's irrelevant here — the permanent is a creature because it copies Streetbreaker Wurm, and it's also an artifact because of Mycosynth Lattice. It entered the battlefield this turn, so it has summoning sickness (it can't attack or use {T} abilities this turn).

6. Alvin's original Dance of the Dead on the real Streetbreaker Wurm is untouched; that Wurm is still enchanted, +1/+1, and doesn't untap normally.

Timing note: as written, the activation is described during Eureka's resolution, which isn't actually possible — I'm assuming Alvin activated the {1}{U}{R} ability after Eureka finished resolving and after the Aura-copy's trigger had already put Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield. If instead the copy ability had resolved before Viashino Warrior was put onto the battlefield, the Dance of the Dead text (and thus the pending trigger's effect) would already be gone from that permanent and Viashino Warrior would never have left the graveyard.

Player count: nothing here changes between two players and more; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that Eureka's "starting with you, each player may put a permanent card" proceeds in turn order, and simultaneous choices are made in APNAP order (101.4).

question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?
answer:
Ari ends up with three green Ooze creatures on the battlefield, none of which has any abilities: two nonlegendary token copies that are 1/1 and 2/2, and the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze (legendary) at 3/3.

How that happens:

1. Storm: two spells were cast before Aeve, Progenitor Ooze this turn, so storm makes two copies, and those copies become tokens. The copies resolve first, one at a time, then the original spell (Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2; 608.1, 608.3a).

2. Counters still get placed. Humility only affects creatures on the battlefield; while Aeve, Progenitor Ooze and its copies are still spells on the stack they keep "Aeve enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each other Ooze you control," and that replacement ability applies as each one enters. Assuming Ari controlled no other Oozes beforehand: first token enters with 0 counters, second token with 1 counter, and the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze with 2 counters (Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2).

3. Layers (613.1a, 613.1g, 613.5, 613.7): Layer 4 – "Aeve isn't legendary if it's a token" is a type/supertype effect applied in layer 4, before Humility strips abilities in layer 6, so both tokens are nonlegendary (and per 613.6-style continuation, that already-applying effect keeps applying). Layer 6 – Humility removes all abilities from all three. Layer 7b – Humility sets base power/toughness to 1/1. Layer 7c – +1/+1 counters apply on top: token A 1/1, token B 2/2, original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze 3/3. The tool-checked resolution for the original confirms 3/3 with no abilities.

4. State-based actions: nothing dies (all have toughness ≥ 1), and the "legend rule" isn't triggered because only the original is legendary — the two tokens lost their legendary supertype in layer 4 (704.4 for the general point that SBAs only look at the game state after resolution).

Timing note: I'm assuming Humility was already on the battlefield when the Aeve, Progenitor Ooze spell and its copies resolved. If Humility instead arrived after they were already on the battlefield, the counters would already be there and the result is the same 1/1, 2/2, 3/3, because Humility's layer 7b effect is always applied before counters in 7c regardless of timestamp (613.5).

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — Humility affects all creatures regardless of controller, and Ari's board is the same whether Nadia is the only opponent or one of several.
